newsitem.title: BELARUS: Key facts about ex-Soviet republic of Belarus.
newsitem.headline: Key facts about ex-Soviet republic of Belarus.

text.p: These are the key facts about the former Soviet republic of Belarus, whose President Alexander Lukashenko signed a Union Treaty with his Russian counterpart Boris Yeltsin in Moscow on Wednesday.
POPULATION: 10.25 million. A breakdown from 1990 shows 77.9 percent Belarussians, 13.2 percent Russians, 4.1 percent Poles, 2.9 percent Ukrainians and 1.1 percent Jews.
AREA: 207,600 sq km (80,200 sq miles). Belarus borders on Poland to the west and Lithuania and Latvia to the north and northwest. To the south lies Ukraine, to the east Russia.
CAPITAL: Minsk, population 1.6 million.

ECONOMY: Along with Ukraine and Russia, Belarus is one of the three "Slav heartland" republics which made up the core of the former Soviet Union. It was a farming and technological base under Kremlin rule, but firms have suffered since independence in December 1991 and output has slumped.
Its factories were noted for heavy-duty trucks, tractors, machine tools and agricultural machinery.
Belarus is also an agricultural region, producing potatoes and vegetables, sugar beet, flax and grain. Agriculture remains highly collectivised.

The republic's currency is the rouble, which has declined to around 4.34 to the Russian rouble since the two currencies were decoupled. Monthly inflation was 6.6 percent in February 1997. Belarus has large debts for Russian energy supplies.
RELIGION: Mainly Russian Orthodox, but there are also large Roman Catholic and eastern rite Catholic communities.

LANGUAGE: Communist rule virtually extinguished the Belarussian language, an eastern Slav tongue similar to Russian, Ukrainian and Polish. Most people now speak Russian and only four percent of the population speak Belarussian regularly.
HISTORY: In its seven centuries of existence Belarus (which means "White Russia") has come mainly under the influence of its neighbours Poland and Russia.

It had no real experience of independent statehood before 1991, although the Belarussian National Convention briefly proclaimed independence between 1917 and 1919 before being divided up between Poland and the Soviet Union.

The 1939 Nazi-Soviet pact which dismembered Poland meant the Soviet Union could take the whole of Belarus back. But when Germany attacked the USSR in 1941, Belarus was overrun. During the Nazi occupation 25 percent of the population died. Industry and agriculture were destroyed.

In the post-war days, Belarus became one of the most hardline republics and the Belarussian Communist Party was dominated by a group of former World War Two anti-Nazi partisans. It won its own seat in the United Nations, but always toed Moscow's line.
Fallout from the 1986 explosion at Ukraine's Chernobyl nuclear station set off a political reaction and authorities eventually had to admit a third of Belarus was contaminated.

The Belarussian Popular Front (BPF), an opposition group, capitalised on the disaster to stage large demonstrations. Nationalist sentiment surged again after the failed August 1991 Kremlin coup against Soviet president Mikhail Gorbachev.
Non-communist professor Stanislav Shushkevich hosted the December 1991 meeting with the leaders of Ukraine and Russia at Belovezhskaya Pushcha near Brest which proclaimed the end of the Soviet Union.

But Shushkevich's attempts to introduce reforms met resistance from conservatives and he was ousted as chairman of parliament in January 1994. A presidential election in July 1994 was won by maverick outsider and anti-corruption campaigner, Alexander Lukashenko.

Lukashenko, who has increased state controls and curbed press freedoms, won sweeping powers in controversial constitutional referendum last November. He set up a new two-chamber parliament of loyalists and appointed a tame constitutional court.
His bid for closer ties with Russia plays on nostalgia for the Soviet days amongst a population whose sense of national identity is weak.
Belarus is the only European state outside former Yugoslavia which has yet to join the Council of Europe.
Belarus is part of NATO's Partnership for Peace programme, but does not take part in joint actions with the alliance or other Soviet block states.
